abstract: What does even a short scrolling 'snack' do to the brain? Short-form video feeds such as Instagram Reels have been rapidly becoming a near-universal phenomenon, used widely by people around the world, especially young adults. However, this is a very recent development, and yet their immediate effects on brain activity, attention, and working memory remain unclear. In a counterbalanced, within-subject experiment, we examined whether 10 minutes of Instagram Reels altered electroencephalographic (EEG) activity, cognitive performance, and subjective fatigue. Thirty university students completed three testing blocks separated by two counterbalanced interventions selected from viewing Reels on their own accounts, viewing a silent sequence of neutral images on their phones, or resting with eyes closed. EEG was recorded using 65 electrodes during interventions and subsequent sustained-attention (SART) and working-memory (N-back) tasks. Compared with neutral images, Reels viewing was associated with higher posterior relative theta power and a lower posterior alpha-to-theta ratio. During the subsequent N-back, frontal relative alpha was higher after Reels than after neutral images. Fatigue increased more after Reels than after rest. One of four planned contrasts in the cleaned sample was significant. Brief Reels viewing was associated with differences in EEG activity compared with viewing neutral images, while no significant differences in attention or working-memory performance were detected after correction for multiple comparisons.
